propositions.text: Consider and clarify Criminal Code regime governing bail pending appeal for serious crime convictions.
Principles guiding appellate courts on bail pending appeal for convicted persons.
Dennis James Oland is appellant convicted of serious crime seeking bail pending appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court introduces the issue of bail pending appeal for serious crime convictions, focusing on appellant Dennis James Oland.

propositions.text: Debate focuses on interpretation of Criminal Code ss. 679(3) and 680(1).
Section 679(3) allows release pending appeal if appellant shows appeal is not frivolous, will surrender, and detention not necessary in public interest.
Section 680(1) allows review of judge's decision under s. 679 by court of appeal, which may vary or substitute decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the relevant Criminal Code provisions governing bail pending appeal and their criteria.

propositions.text: Oland applied for bail pending appeal after second degree murder conviction.
Application denied under public interest criterion; public safety not at issue but public confidence was.
Review panel upheld detention, finding no error in appeal judge's decision.

paragraphs.summary: Oland's bail application was denied on public interest grounds; review panel upheld this decision.

propositions.text: Detaining Oland on public interest grounds was clearly unwarranted.
Appeal judge made material legal error affecting outcome.
Review panel erred in failing to intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds detention unwarranted, identifies legal error by appeal judge, and faults review panel for not intervening.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal of New Brunswick allowed Oland's appeal and ordered new trial before this Court's hearing.
Oland released on bail pending re-trial after Court of Appeal decision.
Appeal to this Court rendered moot but heard on merits; appeal allowed with no further order.

paragraphs.summary: Oland's appeal was allowed by Court of Appeal, he was released, and this Court heard the moot appeal and allowed it with no order.

propositions.text: Richard Oland was found murdered July 7, 2011; Dennis Oland became primary suspect.
Dennis Oland arrested and charged with second degree murder November 12, 2013.

paragraphs.summary: Richard Oland was murdered in 2011; Dennis Oland was arrested and charged in 2013.

propositions.text: Oland released on bail November 18, 2013, with $50,000 surety and conditions.
Convicted of second degree murder December 19, 2015, after three-month trial.
Sentenced February 11, 2016, to life imprisonment with no parole for 10 years.

paragraphs.summary: Oland was released on bail in 2013, convicted in 2015, and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2016.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Oland well-educated, devoted family man without criminal past.
Oland posed no realistic future danger and had excellent reintegration prospects.
Crime was brutal but spontaneous, with lower moral culpability closer to manslaughter.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found Oland a good character posing no danger; crime was brutal but less culpable.

propositions.text: Oland filed notice of appeal January 20, 2016, raising errors in jury charge, evidence, and verdict reasonableness.
Applied for bail pending appeal under s. 679(3) at same time.
Outcome of bail application is focus of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Oland appealed conviction and applied for bail pending appeal; bail application outcome is focus here.

propositions.text: Bail application heard by single Court of Appeal judge; Oland filed affidavits of good character and sureties.
Submitted trial transcript excerpts relevant to grounds of appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Oland supported bail application with affidavits and trial transcript excerpts before single appeal judge.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found Oland met criteria that appeal was not frivolous and would surrender.
Appeal judge considered public interest criterion, dividing it into public safety and public confidence.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal judge found Oland met first two criteria and considered public interest in two parts.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found Oland posed no danger to public, adopting sentencing judge's findings.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal judge found no public safety risk from Oland, adopting sentencing judge's findings.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found gravity and brutality of offence favored detention.
Grounds of appeal were arguable but not strong enough to assure new trial or acquittal.
Appeal judge not persuaded public confidence would be maintained if Oland released; dismissed bail application.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal judge found offence gravity favored detention and dismissed bail application due to public confidence concerns.

propositions.text: Oland applied under s. 680(1) for review of detention order before three-judge panel.

paragraphs.summary: Oland applied for review of detention order by three-judge panel under s. 680(1).

propositions.text: Review panel adopted deferential approach, viewing detention decision as judgment call.
Panel recognized grounds of appeal were serious but Oland convicted of brutal murder with mandatory life sentence.
Denying bail would not render appeal pointless.
Oland failed to show error in appeal judge's reasons or that detention was clearly unreasonable.
Application for review dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Review panel deferred to appeal judge, found no error or unreasonableness, and dismissed review application.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal of New Brunswick allowed Oland's appeal and ordered new trial October 24, 2016.
Oland granted bail pending re-trial October 25, 2016.
Parties alerted to address mootness issue due to these events.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal allowed Oland's appeal and bail pending re-trial; mootness issue raised.

propositions.text: Court raised mootness issue at hearing start; parties urged hearing on merits.
Oland submitted decision significant as same situation may recur after re-trial.
Crown agreed decision significant for future similar situations.
All submitted guidance needed to resolve inconsistent appellate bail approaches.
Borowski and McNeil support hearing moot appeals meeting criteria for public importance and adverseness.

paragraphs.summary: Court raised mootness; parties and interveners urged hearing on merits for guidance and future significance.

propositions.text: Court determined to hear appeal on merits due to unanimous party position and Borowski criteria met.

paragraphs.summary: Court decided to hear appeal on merits given unanimous support and Borowski criteria.

propositions.text: Three statutory criteria for bail pending appeal are in s. 679(3): appeal not frivolous, surrender, and detention not necessary in public interest.
Applicant bears burden to prove each criterion on balance of probabilities, citing cases.

paragraphs.summary: Court states statutory criteria for bail pending appeal and burden of proof on applicant.

propositions.text: First criterion requires appeal judge to ensure grounds of appeal are not frivolous.
Not frivolous test is a very low bar, supported by case law and legal commentary.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains first criterion 'not frivolous' is a low bar supported by case law and commentary.

propositions.text: Applicant must show he will surrender into custody per release order terms (s. 679(3)(b))
Appeal judge must be satisfied applicant will not flee and will surrender as required

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant must show he will surrender into custody and not flee as required by s. 679(3)(b).

propositions.text: Applicant must establish detention is not necessary in the public interest (s. 679(3)(c))
Mr. Oland's bail pending appeal failed on the public interest criterion
Parties seek guidance on considering strength of grounds of appeal in public interest detention analysis

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the public interest criterion and that Mr. Oland failed on it; parties seek guidance on strength of appeal grounds in this context.

propositions.text: In R. v. Farinacci, public interest criterion has two components: public safety and public confidence

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Farinacci found public interest criterion includes public safety and public confidence components.

propositions.text: Public safety relates to protection of the public and tracks secondary ground for release pending trial
Public confidence involves weighing enforceability and reviewability interests

paragraphs.summary: The court states Farinacci found public safety relates to protection, while public confidence weighs enforceability and reviewability.

propositions.text: Enforceability reflects need for immediate enforceability of judgments
Reviewability reflects society's recognition of justice system fallibility and need for meaningful review

paragraphs.summary: The court explains enforceability means respecting immediate judgment enforcement; reviewability means allowing meaningful appeal review.

propositions.text: Farinacci framework has withstood time and is universally endorsed by appellate courts
All parties and interveners accept Farinacci framework and none seek to revisit it
Farinacci remains good law

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Farinacci is still good law, universally endorsed, and accepted by all parties here.

propositions.text: Public safety and public confidence components are not silos and should be considered together
Public safety alone can warrant detention, but residual concerns remain relevant in public confidence analysis

paragraphs.summary: The court finds public safety and confidence components overlap; residual safety concerns remain relevant in confidence analysis.

propositions.text: Difficulty arises in applying Farinacci when public confidence component is raised
Appellate judges struggle balancing enforceability and reviewability in serious crime and strong bail candidate cases

paragraphs.summary: The court notes appellate judges struggle applying Farinacci's public confidence component in serious crime and strong bail cases.

propositions.text: Cases involving public confidence component are rare exceptions in bail pending appeal applications
Porisky states not every offence requires merits assessment; public confidence raised only for serious offences

paragraphs.summary: The court states public confidence issues are rare and Porisky advises raising it only for serious offences.

propositions.text: Court proposes to elaborate on enforceability and reviewability interests to guide appellate judges

paragraphs.summary: The court proposes elaborating on enforceability and reviewability to guide appellate judges in public confidence cases.

propositions.text: Parliament provides factors in s. 515(10)(c) for bail pending trial public confidence assessment
Section 515(10)(c) lists four factors: strength of prosecution case, gravity of offence, circumstances including firearm use, potential lengthy imprisonment

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 515(10)(c) lists four factors for bail pending trial public confidence assessment.

propositions.text: While tailored to pre-trial, s. 515(10)(c) factors have corollary in appellate context with modifications
These factors should be considered in assessing release pending appeal's effect on public confidence

paragraphs.summary: The court argues s. 515(10)(c) factors, suitably modified, should inform public confidence analysis for bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Using s. 515(10)(c) factors promotes consistency and harmony between trial and appellate bail contexts
This approach fosters fairness, coherence, and enhances public confidence in justice administration

paragraphs.summary: The court argues applying s. 515(10)(c) factors promotes consistency and fairness, enhancing public confidence in justice.

propositions.text: Greater bail accessibility pre-trial is rooted in presumption of innocence
Charter s. 11(e) guarantees right not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause

paragraphs.summary: The court states bail is more accessible pre-trial due to presumption of innocence and Charter s. 11(e) rights.

propositions.text: Post-conviction, presumption of innocence is displaced and s. 11(e) no longer applies
Onus shifts to applicant for bail pending appeal, unlike pre-trial where Crown bears onus

paragraphs.summary: The court explains post-conviction bail applicants bear the onus, unlike pre-trial where Crown must justify detention.

propositions.text: Court will explain how s. 515(10)(c) factors inform public confidence component in s. 679(3)(c)

paragraphs.summary: The court will explain how s. 515(10)(c) factors inform public confidence under s. 679(3)(c).

propositions.text: Seriousness of crime plays important role in public confidence concerns for pre-trial detention
Seriousness of crime should equally inform enforceability interest in bail pending appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court finds crime seriousness important for public confidence and enforceability in bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Parliament identifies gravity, circumstances, and potential imprisonment length as seriousness factors in s. 515(10)(c)
These factors are transferable to s. 679(3)(c) with trial judge's sentencing reasons aiding appeal judge
Appeal judge need not repeat trial judge's exercise on seriousness factors as a rule

paragraphs.summary: The court finds seriousness factors in s. 515(10)(c) transferable to s. 679(3)(c); appeal judge relies on trial judge's reasons.

propositions.text: Other factors like residual public safety concerns and flight risks remain relevant under public confidence
Rhyason and Roussin support considering residual risks in public confidence analysis
Absence of flight or safety risks attenuates enforceability interest

paragraphs.summary: The court finds residual safety and flight risks relevant to public confidence; absence of risks reduces enforceability interest.

propositions.text: Strength of prosecution's case under s. 515(10)(c)(i) translates to strength of grounds of appeal in appellate context
Strength of appeal plays central role in assessing reviewability interest
Some authorities express concern about assessing appeal merits beyond s. 679(3)(a) 'not frivolous' criterion
Court does not see problem with assessing appeal strength beyond 'not frivolous' criterion

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appeal strength central to reviewability, rejects concerns about merits assessment beyond 'not frivolous' criterion.

propositions.text: Allowing a pointed consideration of appeal strength does not render the 'not frivolous' criterion meaningless.
The 'not frivolous' criterion is an initial hurdle producing a categorical yes or no answer to reject baseless appeals immediately.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that assessing appeal strength does not negate the 'not frivolous' criterion, which acts as an initial hurdle to reject baseless appeals.

propositions.text: Justice Donald in Porisky states 'not frivolous' and 'sufficient merit' do not foreclose merit consideration beyond threshold tests.
Farinacci set limits on public interest, using merits assessment differently from threshold test.
No redundancy exists; merits can be considered as part of public confidence question.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Justice Donald's Porisky reasoning that merits can be considered beyond threshold tests without redundancy, especially for public confidence.

propositions.text: Justice Trotter explains serious offences require probing inquiry into appeal chances beyond frivolous test.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Justice Trotter's article advocating a probing inquiry into appeal strength for serious offences beyond frivolousness.

propositions.text: Appellate judges assess grounds of appeal for legal plausibility and record foundation to surpass 'not frivolous' criterion.
Categories like 'prospect of success' are unhelpful and may complicate assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellate judges assess appeal grounds for plausibility to meet 'not frivolous' and rejects grading categories as unhelpful.

propositions.text: Appellate judges form preliminary assessments based on counsel materials and relevant authorities, not guesswork.
Review process maintains public confidence and transcends individual interests.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellate judges base assessments on materials and that review maintains public confidence beyond individual cases.

propositions.text: Remedy sought on appeal may lessen reviewability interest, e.g., murder conviction reduced to manslaughter.
Cites cases supporting that lesser remedies reduce reviewability interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that the remedy sought can lessen reviewability interest, citing supporting cases.

propositions.text: Appellate judges must evaluate public confidence factors through eyes of reasonable, informed, dispassionate public member.
Cites R. v. St-Cloud for public confidence standard.
Public confidence differs from uninformed public opinion, which has no role in bail decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellate judges evaluate public confidence through a reasonable public lens, citing St-Cloud, excluding uninformed opinion.

propositions.text: Appellate judges consider appeal delay relative to sentence length in balancing enforceability and reviewability.
Cites R. v. Baltovich on delay consideration.
If bail is impossible, judges should consider expediting appeal under s. 679(10) to preserve reviewability.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judges consider appeal delay and may expedite appeals to preserve reviewability, citing Baltovich.

propositions.text: No precise formula exists for balancing enforceability and reviewability; qualitative contextual assessment required.
Rejects categorical approach to murder or serious offences proposed by interveners.
Principles discussed should be applied uniformly.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects categorical approaches and requires uniform qualitative assessment balancing enforceability and reviewability.

propositions.text: For murder or serious crimes, public interest in enforceability is high and often outweighs reviewability, especially with safety or flight concerns or weak grounds.
Cites R. v. Mapara, Baltovich, Parsons supporting this principle.

paragraphs.summary: The court states enforceability interest usually outweighs reviewability for serious crimes with safety or flight concerns, citing cases.

propositions.text: Where safety or flight concerns are negligible and grounds surpass 'not frivolous', reviewability may outweigh enforceability even for serious offences.

paragraphs.summary: The court states reviewability may outweigh enforceability when safety concerns are negligible and grounds surpass 'not frivolous'.

propositions.text: Before applying principles, will address review hearing principles under s. 680(1) of the Code.

paragraphs.summary: The court will address s. 680(1) review hearing principles before applying earlier principles to the case.

propositions.text: s. 680(1) reviews orders of single Court of Appeal judges under s. 679(3) and some pre-trial bail orders by superior court judges.
s. 680(1) reproduced, allowing review by court on chief justice direction with power to vary or substitute decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 680(1) reviews single judge orders and reproduces the provision's text.

propositions.text: Review process has two stages: chief justice initial vetting, then court review if directed.
Review usually by three-judge panel as in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes s. 680(1) review as two-stage: chief justice vetting and panel review, usually by three judges.

propositions.text: Chief justice's screening considers review nature and standard; panel's mandate addressed first.

paragraphs.summary: The court will address the panel's mandate before the chief justice's screening function under s. 680(1).

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 680(1) panel review should apply correctness standard with independent determination.
Crown and Attorneys General argue for deferential standard requiring legal error before intervention.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue for correctness standard on s. 680(1) review; Crown and AGs argue for deferential standard.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA cite ss. 520 and 521 bail review provisions requiring 'show cause' and argue s. 680(1) lacks this, implying less deference.
They rely on St-Cloud observation that 'show cause' signals deferential approach at trial stage, absent in s. 680(1).

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 680(1) review is less deferential than trial bail reviews, citing 'show cause' absence and St-Cloud.

propositions.text: Court rejects argument that absence of 'show cause' in s. 680(1) implies less deference.
More explicit language would be expected if Parliament intended panel to substitute opinion without more.
Notes St-Cloud para. 104 comments not determinative of s. 680(1) review type.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects that s. 680(1) review is less deferential due to 'show cause' absence, noting St-Cloud comments are not determinative.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c) depends on robust correctness review, citing Farinacci.
They quote Arbour J.A. in Farinacci on correctness standard preventing personal predilections.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 679(3)(c) constitutionality requires correctness review, citing Farinacci's Arbour J.A.

propositions.text: Court finds Farinacci reference unpersuasive as it concerned constitutionality not at issue here.
Correctness is not the only meaningful review form protecting against vagueness.
Comments of Court of Appeal in Farinacci not dispositive on s. 680(1) review nature absent constitutional challenge.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Farinacci reference unpersuasive and that correctness is not the only meaningful review form for s. 680(1).

propositions.text: A panel reviewing a single judge's decision under s. 680(1) should follow three principles guiding deference and intervention.
First, absent palpable and overriding error, the panel must defer to the judge's findings of fact.
Second, the panel may intervene if the judge erred in law or principle and the error was material to the outcome.
Third, without legal error, the panel may intervene if the decision was clearly unwarranted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states three principles for panel review under s. 680(1): defer to fact findings absent error, intervene for material legal error, or if decision is clearly unwarranted.

propositions.text: This approach balances meaningful review with deference to the judge's decision.
It aligns review processes at trial and appeal stages except for s. 469 offences governed by s. 680(1).
Gary T. Trotter explains that endorsing correctness for s. 680 creates differential review standards for s. 469 vs. non-469 offences.
No principled reason supports broader review for murder charges under s. 680 than for manslaughter or attempted murder under s. 520.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the approach balances review and deference, aligns trial and appeal review, citing Trotter on avoiding differential standards for serious offences.

propositions.text: No formal Code procedure governs the chief justice's decision to direct a panel review.
Courts of appeal have adopted different approaches and formality levels for this decision.
Procedural aspects of the gatekeeping function are not before the court and will not be addressed.
Some guidance can be given on the test a chief justice should apply to direct a panel review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no formal procedure governs the chief justice's panel review decision, different approaches exist, and guidance on the test is provided.

propositions.text: The chief justice should direct a review where it is arguable the judge made material errors of fact or law or the decision was clearly unwarranted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the chief justice should direct a review if material errors or a clearly unwarranted decision are arguable.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland was an ideal candidate for bail aside from the seriousness of his offence.
The appeal judge rightly ignored Mr. Oland's prominence and uninformed public opinion.
Mr. Oland was entitled to the same treatment as a less prominent person.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Oland was an ideal bail candidate, with the appeal judge rightly ignoring his prominence and public opinion.

propositions.text: If Mr. Oland did not qualify for release, no one convicted of similarly serious offences would be released without unique or strong appeal grounds.
Parliament did not restrict bail pending appeal for murder or serious crimes; courts should respect this.
For s. 679(3)(c), even serious offences may warrant release if no public safety or flight concerns and grounds surpass 'not frivolous'.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues serious offenders would never be released without unique grounds; the court states Parliament allows bail pending appeal if criteria met.

propositions.text: Each case requires contextual analysis considering factors like criminal record, public safety, flight risk, and release plan.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a contextual analysis is required considering various factors for bail decisions.

propositions.text: The appeal judge found no public safety or flight risk concerns and grounds of appeal were 'clearly arguable'.
These findings are not challenged on appeal.
The trial judge found Mr. Oland's crime gravitated more toward manslaughter than first degree murder.
This finding lessened moral blameworthiness and attenuated the crime's seriousness and enforceability interest.
The cumulative effect should have favored release; detention was clearly unwarranted and Court of Appeal erred in not intervening.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appeal judge's unchallenged findings and trial judge's manslaughter finding lessen seriousness, making detention clearly unwarranted.

propositions.text: The appeal judge erred by requiring more than 'clearly arguable' grounds, seeking unique circumstances assuring new trial or acquittal.
The appeal judge balanced offence seriousness and brutality against factors favoring release, concluding public confidence would be undermined.
The court respectfully disagrees and holds 'clearly arguable' grounds suffice to surpass 'not frivolous' criterion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appeal judge erred by requiring unique circumstances beyond 'clearly arguable' grounds, which suffice to surpass 'not frivolous'.

propositions.text: Had the appeal not been moot, the court would have set aside detention and ordered release pending appeal.
Because the appeal is moot, the court allows the appeal and makes no further order.

paragraphs.summary: The court would have ordered release but allows the moot appeal with no further order.
